opus-5.5.text:
I think it makes a lot of sense, especially at the very early stage. When a company is just starting out, there's often not much else to evaluate. The product may not exist yet, the market may still be forming, and the original idea will probably change several times. What stays constant is the team: how they think, how fast they learn, and whether they can keep going when things don't work.

From my own experience on the technical side, especially in AI infrastructure and systems, the field moves incredibly fast. Something that looks like a strong technical edge today can be commoditized in six months. So I think a good investor is really betting on whether the founders understand the problem deeply enough to stay ahead of that curve. Can they spot where things are heading before everyone else does? Can they attract other strong people to work with them? Those things are hard to fake, and they compound over time.

That said, I don't think "investing in people" should become an excuse to ignore fundamentals. Sometimes it turns into pattern-matching: this person went to a certain school, or worked at a famous company, so they must be a good bet. That's not really evaluating the person, it's evaluating their résumé. The more meaningful signals are things like clarity of thinking, intellectual honesty, and how they've handled hard problems before. Have they built something real? Do they admit what they don't know?

So my view is that people are the most important factor early on, but you have to look at them seriously and with substance, not just at their credentials. And as a company matures, the balance naturally shifts toward traction, product, and business metrics. At the very beginning, though, you're mostly backing a team and their ability to figure things out.

r001.rationale: It says that as a company matures, attention shifts toward traction, product, and business metrics.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most honest ways to invest, especially at the early stage, because at that point there's almost nothing else to evaluate. There's no revenue, often no product, and the market analysis in the deck is mostly a story the founders are telling themselves. What you actually have in front of you is a person, and the question is whether that person can keep learning faster than the problem changes.

What I look for is a few things. One is how someone thinks about their own mistakes. If a founder can tell me in detail about a decision they got wrong and what they'd do differently, that's usually a better signal than any pitch. Two is whether they have what I'd call earned conviction, meaning they've spent real time close to the problem, either as a user, a builder, or a researcher, and their confidence comes from that rather than from a trend. And three is how they treat people when nothing is at stake, like how they talk about former colleagues or cofounders who left.

The risk with people-first investing is that it can slide into pattern matching on charisma or pedigree, which is really just bias with a nicer name. So I try to separate "I like this person" from "this person is structurally suited to this problem." Those overlap less than you'd think. A brilliant systems researcher might be exactly wrong for a consumer product, and a scrappy operator might be the perfect fit for an unglamorous infrastructure business.

I'd also say the people lens matters more the longer the time horizon. Markets shift, products pivot, but the founder is the one constant in the company for ten years. If I'm going to be wrong about the market, which I often am, I'd rather be wrong alongside someone who can find their way out of it.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on early-stage investing and founder qualities; it does not say investors may emphasize quantitative business results in later funding rounds.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss first-round investors, evaluating the venture alongside its founders, or an open-source foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think investing in people is important, especially at the early stage, when the product and business model may still change. But “betting on the founder” needs to mean something concrete. What gives this person an unusual understanding of the problem? Can they attract a strong team? And when reality contradicts their assumptions, can they learn and adjust?

Confidence and storytelling can make a strong first impression, but I’d want to understand how someone actually makes decisions and follows through. You also have to look at the opportunity itself. A capable founder still needs a real customer need and a viable business. For me, the question is how well this particular person fits this particular problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investing in people at the early stage but does not say that later-round investors may focus on quantitative business results.

r002.rationale: The response considers the opportunity alongside the founder, but does not mention first-round investors or attribute that consideration to an open-source foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think investing in people is important, especially at an early stage, when the product and business model may still change. But it has to mean more than liking a founder or being impressed by their résumé. I want to understand how they think, how deeply they know the problem, and how they respond when reality challenges their assumptions.

Confidence is easy to see in a pitch. Judgment, honesty, and the ability to learn take longer to assess. Can they acknowledge what they don’t know? Can they attract good people? When something goes wrong, do they take responsibility and adapt? Those are the qualities that make investing in the person meaningful to me.
